rules.title: The cramfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The cramfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A cramfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling cramfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The freevxfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The freevxfs filesystem is a free implementation of the Veritas filesystem and is the primary filesystem type used on HP-UX systems.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling freevxfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfs filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem that allows Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The hfsplus kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The hfsplus filesystem is a hierarchical filesystem designed to succeed hfs, enabling Macintosh (Mac OS) volumes to be mounted on Linux.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling hfsplus when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The jffs2 kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The jffs2 (Journaling Flash File System 2) filesystem is a journaling filesystem designed for use on flash memory devices.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling jffs2 when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The overlay kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The overlay kernel module (OverlayFS) provides a union-mount filesystem that combines an upper and lower filesystem into a single unified view.
rules.impact: The overlay kernel module has known CVEs: CVE-2023-32629, CVE-2023-2640, and CVE-2023-0386. Disabling unused OverlayFS support reduces the local attack surface and mitigates risks related to unauthorized setuid file execution.

rules.title: The squashfs kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The squashfs filesystem is a compressed, read-only filesystem intended for systems with limited memory. A squashfs image can be mounted and used without first decompressing the image.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling squashfs when it is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The udf kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: The udf filesystem implements the Universal Disk Format (ISO/IEC 13346 and ECMA-167), an open format used to store data on a wide range of media, including DVD and newer optical discs.
rules.impact: Removing support for unused filesystem types reduces the local attack surface. Disabling udf when optical media support is not required limits opportunities for filesystem-related exploits.

rules.title: The FireWire (IEEE 1394) kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: IEEE 1394 (FireWire) is a serial bus standard for high-speed, real-time device communication.
rules.impact: Disabling FireWire support reduces the physical and driver attack surface and protects the system from exploitation of flaws in the FireWire implementation.

rules.title: The USB storage kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: USB storage devices allow portable transfer and retention of files independent of network connectivity. Their widespread use has also made USB media a common vector for introducing malware and establishing persistent access.
rules.impact: Restricting USB storage access reduces the physical attack surface and limits a common path for malware introduction into the environment.

rules.title: Unused filesystem kernel modules are not available
rules.explanation: Filesystem kernel modules are loadable kernel components that add support for specific filesystem types. Unused filesystem modules expand the set of code that can be loaded into the running kernel.
rules.impact: Attackers on a compromised system can abuse unused filesystem kernel modules to hide processes or files. Removing unused filesystem modules reduces the local attack surface and limits a common rootkit technique.

rules.title: /tmp is a separate partition or tmpfs
rules.explanation: The /tmp directory is a world-writable location used for temporary storage by users and applications.
rules.impact: Mounting /tmp as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, reducing the risk that an attacker can stage and run executable code from /tmp. It also helps prevent hard-link based attacks against setuid programs that may be updated on the system.
rules.scope: Settings in /etc/fstab and systemd unit files

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /tmp and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying nosuid prevents users from introducing setuid binaries in /tmp that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute malicious binaries staged in /tmp.

rules.title: /dev/shm is a separate partition or tmpfs
rules.explanation: The /dev/shm directory is a world-writable shared-memory filesystem commonly used for inter-process communication (IPC).
rules.impact: Mounting /dev/shm as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, reducing the risk that an attacker can place and run executable code in shared memory. It also helps prevent hard-link based attacks against setuid programs.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /dev/shm is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating special devices on /dev/shm and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying nosuid on /dev/shm prevents introduction of privileged programs via shared memory that could be executed by non-root users, reducing privilege-escalation risk.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /dev/shm
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Applying noexec on /dev/shm prevents execution of programs from shared memory, reducing the risk that users introduce and run malicious software from this location.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /home
rules.explanation: The /home directory provides disk space for local user data and home directories.
rules.impact: Default installations often place all data on a single root filesystem. Isolating /home on a separate partition contains user-driven disk growth and reduces the risk that resource exhaustion in /home will fill the root filesystem and disrupt overall system availability.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /home and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /home
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /home is intended for user files, applying nosuid prevents users from creating setuid binaries in /home that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var
rules.explanation: The /var directory is used by daemons and system services for dynamic and temporary data. Some directories under /var may be world-writable.
rules.impact: Placing /var on a separate partition enables additional mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage exploits. Isolation also helps contain growth of variable data so it does not exhaust the root filesystem.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var is intended for variable data such as logs and service state, applying nosuid prevents creation of setuid binaries under /var that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The /var/tmp directory is a world-writable location used for temporary storage by users and applications. Unlike /tmp, files in /var/tmp are expected to persist across reboots.
rules.impact: Mounting /var/tmp as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage and execute exploits from temporary storage.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var/tmp and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying nosuid prevents users from introducing setuid binaries in /var/tmp that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/tmp
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/tmp is intended only for temporary storage, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute malicious binaries staged in /var/tmp.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log
rules.explanation: The /var/log directory is used by system services to store log data.
rules.impact: Mounting /var/log as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage exploits. Isolation also helps prevent log growth from exhausting the root filesystem.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var/log and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is intended only for log files, applying nosuid prevents creation of setuid binaries under /var/log that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log is intended only for log files, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute binaries staged under /var/log.

rules.title: A separate partition exists for /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The audit daemon (auditd) stores its log data under the /var/log/audit directory.
rules.impact: Mounting /var/log/audit as a dedicated filesystem enables restrictive mount options such as noexec, nosuid, and nodev, which limit an attacker's ability to stage exploits. Isolation also helps protect audit log capacity from being exhausted by unrelated filesystem activity.

rules.title: The nodev mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nodev mount option prevents interpretation of character or block special devices on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log/audit is not intended to host device nodes, applying nodev prevents users from creating block or character special devices in /var/log/audit and reduces the risk of device-based attacks.

rules.title: The nosuid mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The nosuid mount option prevents the kernel from honoring the setuid and setgid bits on files on the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log/audit is intended only for audit logs, applying nosuid prevents creation of setuid binaries under /var/log/audit that could be used for privilege escalation.

rules.title: The noexec mount option is set on /var/log/audit
rules.explanation: The noexec mount option prevents execution of binaries from the mounted filesystem.
rules.impact: Because /var/log/audit is intended only for audit logs, applying noexec reduces the risk that an attacker can execute binaries staged under /var/log/audit.

rules.title: GPG keys are configured
rules.explanation: The RPM package manager uses GPG key signatures to verify package integrity during and after installation.
rules.impact: Correctly configured GPG keys help ensure updates come from a trusted source and reduce the risk of spoofing that could lead to unintentional installation of malware.

rules.title: Gpgcheck is configured
rules.explanation: The gpgcheck option controls whether package signatures are verified after download and before installation.
rules.impact: Verifying RPM package signatures before installation ensures software was obtained from a trusted source and reduces the risk of installing tampered packages.

rules.title: Repo_gpgcheck is enabled globally
rules.explanation: The repo_gpgcheck option, set in the main section of /etc/dnf/dnf.conf and in individual /etc/yum.repos.d/* repository files, enables GPG signature verification of repository metadata (repodata).
rules.impact: Verifying repository metadata signatures before use reduces the risk of installing software from tampered repository data.

rules.title: Package manager repositories are configured
rules.explanation: Systems must have appropriate package manager repositories configured so they can receive current patches and updates.
rules.impact: Incorrect repository configuration may prevent delivery of important security patches or allow a rogue repository to introduce compromised software.

rules.title: Weak dependencies are configured
rules.explanation: The RPM packaging specification supports hard dependencies and weak dependencies that may pull in additional packages beyond strictly required components.
rules.impact: If the capabilities provided by weak dependencies are not required, omitting those packages reduces the potential attack surface of the system.

rules.title: Updates, patches, and additional security software are installed
rules.explanation: Operating system and package updates deliver security patches and functional fixes as vendors address newly discovered vulnerabilities and defects.
rules.impact: Unpatched software leaves systems exposed to known vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit. Keeping packages current reduces residual risk from publicly documented flaws.

rules.title: SELinux is installed
rules.explanation: SELinux provides mandatory access control (MAC) in addition to traditional discretionary access control (DAC).
rules.impact: Without a MAC framework installed, the system relies only on default DAC controls, which offer weaker confinement of processes and users.

rules.title: SELinux is not disabled in bootloader configuration
rules.explanation: SELinux must be enabled at boot and must not be overridden by GRUB boot parameters that disable it.
rules.impact: If SELinux is disabled via bootloader parameters, its access controls will not be applied and the intended security posture can be bypassed at boot time.

rules.title: The SELinux policy is configured
rules.explanation: SELinux should be configured to use a policy that meets or exceeds the default targeted policy, which confines daemons and system software.
rules.impact: Sites may require stricter policies than the default, which is acceptable. This control ensures that at least the recommended baseline policy requirements are met so SELinux confinement is effective.

rules.title: SELinux mode is not disabled
rules.explanation: SELinux can operate in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing.
rules.impact: Running SELinux in disabled mode is strongly discouraged. In disabled mode the system neither enforces SELinux policy nor labels persistent objects such as files, which makes enabling SELinux later more difficult and leaves the system without MAC protections.

rules.title: SELinux mode is enforcing
rules.explanation: SELinux can operate in one of three modes: disabled, permissive, or enforcing.
rules.impact: Disabled mode skips both policy enforcement and object labeling, complicating future enablement. Permissive mode logs policy violations but does not block them. Enforcing mode applies SELinux policy and provides the intended mandatory access controls.

rules.title: No unconfined services exist
rules.explanation: Unconfined processes run in unconfined SELinux domains rather than in tightly restricted service domains.
rules.impact: Although some SELinux rules still apply, processes in unconfined domains are granted broad access and largely rely on DAC. If an unconfined process is compromised, SELinux provides limited containment, increasing the risk of unauthorized access to system resources and data. SELinux complements DAC; it does not replace it.
rules.scope: Settings in SELinux policies and configuration

rules.title: The MCS translation service (mcstrans) is not installed
rules.explanation: The mcstransd daemon translates SELinux Multi-Level Security (MLS) and Multi-Category Security (MCS) labels into human-readable form for client processes that request them.
rules.impact: When category label translation is not required, removing mcstrans reduces the amount of potentially vulnerable code and services present on the system.

rules.title: SETroubleshoot is not installed
rules.explanation: SETroubleshoot notifies desktop users of SELinux denials through a graphical interface and can surface information about configuration errors and related issues.
rules.impact: SETroubleshoot is an unnecessary service on most servers, particularly when a graphical desktop (X Window System) is not used, and increases the installed attack surface.

rules.title: A bootloader password is set
rules.explanation: A bootloader password requires authentication before boot command-line parameters can be modified when the system is restarted.
rules.impact: Requiring a bootloader password prevents unauthorized users from altering boot parameters or the boot configuration, including changes that weaken security such as disabling SELinux at boot.

rules.title: Bootloader configuration file permissions are restricted
rules.explanation: GRUB configuration files contain boot settings and may include credentials used to unlock boot options.
rules.impact: Restricting bootloader configuration access to root prevents non-root users from reading or modifying boot parameters. Exposure of boot settings can reveal weaknesses that an attacker could exploit at boot time.

rules.title: Core dump file size is limited
rules.explanation: The core resource limit controls the maximum size of core dump files. A hard limit enforces a ceiling that users cannot raise.
rules.impact: A hard limit on core dumps prevents users from overriding a restrictive soft limit. Core dumps capture process memory at termination and may contain sensitive data, so unconstrained dumps increase the risk of information disclosure.

rules.title: Fs.protected_hardlinks is configured
rules.explanation: The fs.protected_hardlinks sysctl controls whether users may create hard links to files they do not own or cannot write.
rules.impact: Restricting hard link creation mitigates race conditions and TOCTOU-style attacks against privileged programs that operate on files via open or creat, reducing a common local exploitation vector.

rules.title: Fs.protected_symlinks is configured
rules.explanation: The fs.protected_symlinks sysctl controls how the kernel follows symbolic links in world-writable sticky directories and similar sensitive paths.
rules.impact: Restricting unsafe symlink following mitigates race conditions against privileged programs that operate on files via open or creat, reducing a common local exploitation vector.

rules.title: Fs.suid_dumpable is configured
rules.explanation: The fs.suid_dumpable sysctl determines whether setuid or otherwise privileged processes may generate core dumps.
rules.impact: Core dumps from privileged processes may contain sensitive memory contents such as password hashes or cryptographic keys. Restricting dumpable behavior reduces the risk of disclosing that data to an attacker.

rules.title: Kernel.dmesg_restrict is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel.dmesg_restrict sysctl controls whether unprivileged users may read the kernel log (dmesg) buffer.
rules.impact: Restricting the kernel message buffer to privileged users limits reconnaissance by unprivileged attackers who might otherwise harvest sensitive system information from kernel logs.

rules.title: Kernel.kptr_restrict is configured
rules.explanation: The kernel.kptr_restrict sysctl controls whether kernel addresses are exposed through /proc and other interfaces.
rules.impact: Masking kernel pointers, including symbols visible via /proc/kallsyms, reduces an attacker's ability to gather layout information useful for developing or weaponizing kernel exploits.

rules.title: Kernel.yama.ptrace_scope is configured
rules.explanation: The ptrace system call allows one process to observe and control another process, including inspecting and modifying its memory and registers.
rules.impact: If one application is compromised, an attacker may use ptrace to attach to other processes running as the same user and extract additional credentials. Restricting ptrace scope limits lateral movement within a user's process set.

rules.title: Kernel.randomize_va_space is configured
rules.explanation: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is an exploit mitigation technique that randomly arranges key regions of a process address space.
rules.impact: Randomizing virtual memory layout makes memory-corruption exploits more difficult to develop and reuse because target addresses change between executions.

rules.title: Systemd-coredump ProcessSizeMax is configured
rules.explanation: A core dump captures the memory of a running process, typically to diagnose crashes. Core files may also contain sensitive information from process memory.
rules.impact: Limiting the maximum process size handled by systemd-coredump reduces retention of large memory images that may contain sensitive data, lowering the risk of information disclosure from core dumps.

rules.title: Systemd-coredump storage is configured
rules.explanation: A core dump captures the memory of a running process, typically to diagnose crashes. Core files may also contain sensitive information from process memory.
rules.impact: Controlling where and whether systemd-coredump stores core files reduces unnecessary retention of memory images that may contain sensitive data and are primarily useful for debugging.

rules.title: The system-wide cryptographic policy is not set to legacy
rules.explanation: The system-wide cryptographic policy selects allowed cryptographic algorithms for TLS, SSH, and related subsystems. The LEGACY policy maximizes compatibility with older systems at the cost of weaker cryptography.
rules.impact: The LEGACY policy permits obsolete and weakened algorithms. Using a stronger policy reduces exposure to cryptographic attacks that rely on outdated primitives.

rules.title: The system-wide crypto policy disables SHA-1 hashes and signatures
rules.explanation: SHA-1 is a cryptographic hash function that produces a 160-bit digest. System-wide crypto policy can disable SHA-1 for hashing and digital signatures where stronger algorithms are required.
rules.impact: SHA-1 has known practical collision weaknesses. Disabling SHA-1 hashes and signatures reduces the risk of forgery and downgrade attacks against protocols that still offer SHA-1.

rules.title: The system-wide crypto policy MAC algorithms are configured
rules.explanation: A Message Authentication Code (MAC) authenticates message integrity using a symmetric key. The system-wide cryptographic policy can restrict which MAC algorithms are offered by system services.
rules.impact: Weak MAC algorithms can be exploited with sufficient computational resources. Restricting MAC choices to strong algorithms reduces the risk of integrity and authentication failures.

rules.title: The system-wide crypto policy disables CBC for SSH
rules.explanation: Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) is a block cipher mode of operation that has been used with SSH encryption algorithms.
rules.impact: Known weaknesses in SSH using CBC mode may allow an attacker to recover plaintext from ciphertext blocks, increasing the risk of session data exposure.

rules.title: /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after successful logon and serve as the message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: Appropriate warning banners inform users of their legal status regarding system use, including ownership and monitoring policies. Including OS or patch-level details in banners can also disclose reconnaissance information useful to attackers targeting known vulnerabilities.

rules.title: /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before logon on local terminals.
rules.impact: Appropriate warning banners inform users of their legal status regarding system use, including ownership and monitoring policies. Including OS or patch-level details in banners can also disclose reconnaissance information useful to attackers targeting known vulnerabilities.

rules.title: /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before logon for remote connections from configured network services.
rules.impact: Appropriate warning banners inform users of their legal status regarding system use, including ownership and monitoring policies. Including OS or patch-level details in banners can also disclose reconnaissance information useful to attackers targeting known vulnerabilities.

rules.title: Access to /etc/motd is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/motd are displayed to users after successful logon and serve as the message of the day for authenticated users.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions on /etc/motd allow unauthorized users to modify the message of the day with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue are displayed to users before logon on local terminals.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions on /etc/issue allow unauthorized users to modify the local login banner with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: Access to /etc/issue.net is configured
rules.explanation: The contents of /etc/issue.net are displayed to users before logon for remote connections from configured network services.
rules.impact: Incorrect permissions on /etc/issue.net allow unauthorized users to modify the remote login banner with incorrect or misleading information.

rules.title: The GDM login banner is configured
rules.explanation: GDM (GNOME Display Manager) handles graphical login on GNOME-based systems. A login banner displays an organizational warning or legal notice before authentication. dconf lock mode prevents users from overriding the system-defined banner settings.
rules.impact: A login banner informs users of the system owner and applicable monitoring or acceptable-use policies before access is granted. Without locked system settings, user preferences can override the banner and weaken policy enforcement.

rules.title: The GDM disable-user-list setting is configured
rules.explanation: GDM handles graphical login on GNOME-based systems. The disable-user-list parameter controls whether known local accounts are shown on the login screen.
rules.impact: Displaying the user list reveals valid account names and reduces the effort required for unauthorized login attempts. Without locked system settings, users can re-enable the list and undermine this control.

rules.title: GDM screen lock is configured
rules.explanation: GNOME Desktop Manager can automatically lock the screen after a period of user inactivity. Lock settings define when the session is protected and how users must reauthenticate.
rules.impact: Screen lock reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized access to an unattended graphical session. Without locked system settings, users can disable or weaken idle lock behavior.

rules.title: GDM automount is configured
rules.explanation: By default, GNOME can automatically mount removable media when it is inserted. Automount settings control whether media is mounted without explicit user action.
rules.impact: When automounting is enabled, anyone with physical access can connect removable media and make its contents available without separate mount permission. Without locked system settings, users can re-enable automount and increase exposure to untrusted media.

rules.title: GDM autorun-never is configured
rules.explanation: The autorun-never setting disables automatic execution of content when removable media is inserted under GNOME Display Manager.
rules.impact: Malware on removable media can leverage AutoPlay or autorun behavior to execute when media is inserted. Disabling autorun reduces that risk; without locked system settings, users can reverse the control.

rules.title: Xwayland is configured
rules.explanation: Xwayland is a compatibility layer that allows legacy X11 applications to run in a Wayland environment. Its availability determines whether X11 protocol behavior remains reachable on the desktop session.
rules.impact: Wayland security benefits come largely from eliminating the traditional X11 network listener and related attack paths. Enabling Xwayland reintroduces X11 compatibility risks and can weaken those protections.

rules.title: Autofs services are not in use
rules.explanation: autofs automatically mounts filesystems and devices on demand, commonly including CD/DVD and USB media.
rules.impact: When automounting is enabled, anyone with physical access can attach removable media and make its contents available even without explicit mount permission, expanding the local attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package autofs, systemd units

rules.title: Avahi daemon services are not in use
rules.explanation: Avahi is a zeroconf implementation that provides multicast DNS and DNS-SD service discovery. It allows programs to publish and discover hosts and services on a local network without manual configuration.
rules.impact: Automatic network service discovery is rarely required for core system operation and exposes additional network-facing functionality. Removing unused Avahi components reduces the attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package avahi, systemd units

rules.title: Cockpit web services are not in use
rules.explanation: Cockpit provides remote system administration through a web browser interface.
rules.impact: If remote web-based administration is not an approved requirement, Cockpit packages should not remain installed. Removing them reduces the network-facing attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package cockpit-ws, systemd units

rules.title: DHCP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: A DHCP server dynamically assigns IP addresses and related network configuration to clients on a network.
rules.impact: Unless the system is intentionally operated as a DHCP server, retaining server packages such as kea unnecessarily increases the attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package kea, systemd units

rules.title: DNS server services are not in use
rules.explanation: DNS is a hierarchical naming system that maps host and service names to IP addresses for resources on a network.
rules.impact: Unless the system is intended to operate as a DNS server, retaining DNS server packages increases the attack surface without providing required functionality.
rules.scope: Settings in package bind, systemd units

rules.title: Dnsmasq services are not in use
rules.explanation: dnsmasq is a lightweight service that can provide DNS caching, DNS forwarding, and DHCP functions on a host.
rules.impact: If the system is not intended to act as a DNS cache, DNS forwarder, or DHCP server, retaining dnsmasq increases the attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package dnsmasq, systemd units

rules.title: FTP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: FTP is a traditional file-transfer protocol used to move files between clients and servers over a network. Many deployments historically permit anonymous or weakly authenticated access.
rules.impact: If the system is not required to operate as an FTP server, removing the package reduces the attack surface associated with an outdated and poorly protected file-transfer service.
rules.scope: Settings in package vsftpd, systemd units

rules.title: Message access server services are not in use
rules.explanation: dovecot and cyrus-imapd provide IMAP and POP3 mail-access server functionality on Linux systems.
rules.impact: If the system will not provide POP3 or IMAP services, retaining these packages increases the attack surface without operational benefit.
rules.scope: Settings in packages dovecot, cyrus-imapd, systemd units

rules.title: Network File System services are not in use
rules.explanation: Network File System (NFS) allows a host to mount filesystems from remote servers over the network and to export local filesystems to other hosts.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to mount or serve NFS resources, removing NFS packages and services reduces the network attack surface associated with remote filesystem protocols.
rules.scope: Settings in package nfs-utils, systemd units

rules.title: Print server services are not in use
rules.explanation: CUPS provides printing to local and network printers, can accept remote print jobs, and exposes remote administration through a web interface.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to submit or accept print jobs, removing CUPS reduces the attack surface of an unused networked print service.
rules.scope: Settings in package cups, systemd units

rules.title: Rpcbind services are not in use
rules.explanation: rpcbind maps Remote Procedure Call (RPC) services to the ports on which they listen and redirects clients to the correct port. Portmapper is the related RPC service used for this mapping.
rules.impact: Portmapper responses can be abused in amplification-style DDoS attacks. If RPC port mapping is not required, removing rpcbind reduces the attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package rpcbind, systemd units

rules.title: Rsync services are not in use
rules.explanation: The rsyncd service synchronizes files between systems over network connections.
rules.impact: rsyncd commonly communicates without encryption, exposing transferred data and increasing risk if the daemon is reachable. If the service is not required, removing the rsync-daemon package reduces the attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package rsync-daemon, systemd units

rules.title: Samba file server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The Samba daemon enables Linux systems to share filesystems and directories with Windows clients using SMB/CIFS protocols.
rules.impact: If Windows file sharing is not required, removing Samba reduces the attack surface associated with an unused network file server.
rules.scope: Settings in package samba, systemd units

rules.title: SNMP services are not in use
rules.explanation: SNMP is a protocol commonly used to monitor network equipment, hosts, and devices such as UPS units.
rules.impact: SNMP servers may support SNMPv1, which transmits data in cleartext and offers weak authentication. If SNMP is not required, removing net-snmp reduces the attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package net-snmp, systemd units

rules.title: Telnet server services are not in use
rules.explanation: The telnet-server package provides a daemon that accepts remote interactive connections using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: Telnet transmits session data, including credentials, without encryption. Network observers can capture authentication material. Encrypted alternatives such as SSH provide stronger protection.
rules.scope: Settings in package telnet-server, systemd units

rules.title: TFTP server services are not in use
rules.explanation: TFTP is a simple file-transfer protocol used between TCP/IP hosts. A TFTP server allows clients to send and receive files with minimal protocol overhead.
rules.impact: TFTP provides no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication. If the system is not required to operate as a TFTP server, removing the package reduces the attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package tftp-server, systemd units

rules.title: Web proxy server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Squid is a widely used HTTP/HTTPS caching proxy server packaged in many Linux distributions.
rules.impact: Unless the system is intentionally configured as a proxy server, retaining Squid increases the attack surface of an unused network service.
rules.scope: Settings in package squid, systemd units

rules.title: Web server services are not in use
rules.explanation: Web server packages provide the ability to host and serve website or application content over HTTP and related protocols.
rules.impact: If there is no approved requirement to run a web server on the system, removing web server packages reduces the network-facing attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in packages httpd, nginx, systemd units

rules.title: GNOME Display Manager is removed
rules.explanation: GDM manages graphical display servers and handles graphical user logon for GNOME environments.
rules.impact: If a graphical user interface is not required, removing GDM reduces the attack surface associated with unused graphical login components.

rules.title: X Window System services are not in use
rules.explanation: The X Window System provides a graphical user interface in which users can run applications in multiple windows and related desktop components.
rules.impact: If graphical logon and X Window access are not required by organizational policy, removing these services reduces the attack surface.

rules.title: Mail transfer agents are configured for local-only mode
rules.explanation: Mail transfer agents (MTAs) such as Postfix or sendmail accept and deliver mail. Local-only mode limits the MTA to processing mail for the local host rather than accepting inbound network mail.
rules.impact: MTAs are complex and have a long history of security issues. Restricting an MTA to local-only operation reduces remote attack surface while still allowing local mail delivery needed by system utilities.

rules.title: The FTP client is not installed
rules.explanation: The FTP client is a traditional tool for transferring files between systems over a network and may be used with weak or anonymous authentication.
rules.impact: FTP does not protect the confidentiality of data or authentication credentials. Preferring encrypted alternatives such as SFTP, and removing an unused FTP client, reduces exposure of sensitive information and the local attack surface.

rules.title: The LDAP client is not installed
rules.explanation: LDAP provides a method for looking up directory information in a central database and historically replaced NIS/YP for many environments.
rules.impact: If the system does not need to act as an LDAP client, removing the client software reduces the attack surface of unused directory-access tooling.

rules.title: The telnet client is not installed
rules.explanation: The telnet package provides a client that establishes interactive remote sessions using the telnet protocol.
rules.impact: Telnet is unencrypted, so credentials and session data can be intercepted on the network. Encrypted alternatives such as SSH provide stronger protection, and removing an unused telnet client reduces risk.

rules.title: The TFTP client is not installed
rules.explanation: TFTP is a simple protocol for exchanging files between TCP/IP hosts. A TFTP client connects to a TFTP server to send and receive files.
rules.impact: TFTP has no built-in encryption, access control, or authentication, so retaining an unused client increases the risk of insecure file transfers.

rules.title: Time synchronization is in use
rules.explanation: System clocks should be synchronized across hosts in an environment. This is typically achieved by using one or more authoritative time sources and configuring all systems to follow them.
rules.impact: Accurate time supports security mechanisms such as Kerberos and produces consistent log timestamps across systems, which is essential for correlation and forensic investigation.

rules.title: Chrony is configured
rules.explanation: Chrony synchronizes system time using NTP sources. The server directive specifies an individual NTP server, while the pool directive specifies a pool of NTP servers.
rules.impact: Proper chrony configuration helps maintain accurate time for security-sensitive protocols and consistent enterprise-wide log timestamps used in forensic analysis.

rules.title: Chrony is not running as the root user
rules.explanation: The /etc/sysconfig/chronyd file configures chrony startup parameters, including the user account under which the daemon runs. By default, chrony runs as the chrony user.
rules.impact: Running network-facing or privileged services as root increases the impact of a compromise. Ensuring chrony runs as a non-root user limits potential privilege escalation.

rules.title: The cron daemon is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The cron daemon schedules and executes batch jobs on the system according to configured schedules.
rules.impact: Even when user jobs are uncommon, systems rely on scheduled maintenance and security-monitoring tasks. An inactive cron daemon can prevent those controls from running as intended.

rules.title: Access to /etc/crontab is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/crontab file defines system-level cron jobs managed by the cron daemon.
rules.impact: Write access may allow unprivileged users to escalate privileges by inserting malicious jobs. Read access may reveal scheduled system tasks and aid planning of unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Access to /etc/cron.hourly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.hourly directory contains system cron jobs that are intended to run once per hour.
rules.impact: Write access for unprivileged users can enable privilege escalation through malicious scheduled jobs. Read access may reveal how elevated privileges are obtained or how audit controls can be bypassed.

rules.title: Access to /etc/cron.daily is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.daily directory contains system cron jobs that are intended to run once per day.
rules.impact: Write access for unprivileged users can enable privilege escalation through malicious scheduled jobs. Read access may reveal how elevated privileges are obtained or how audit controls can be bypassed.

rules.title: Access to /etc/cron.weekly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.weekly directory contains system cron jobs that are intended to run once per week.
rules.impact: Write access for unprivileged users can enable privilege escalation through malicious scheduled jobs. Read access may reveal how elevated privileges are obtained or how audit controls can be bypassed.

rules.title: Access to /etc/cron.monthly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.monthly directory contains system cron jobs that are intended to run once per month.
rules.impact: Write access for unprivileged users can enable privilege escalation through malicious scheduled jobs. Read access may reveal how elevated privileges are obtained or how audit controls can be bypassed.

rules.title: Access to /etc/cron.yearly is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.yearly directory contains system cron jobs that are intended to run once per year.
rules.impact: Write access for unprivileged users can enable privilege escalation through malicious scheduled jobs. Read access may reveal how elevated privileges are obtained or how audit controls can be bypassed.

rules.title: Access to /etc/cron.d is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/cron.d directory holds additional system cron job definitions with more granular scheduling than the standard hourly, daily, weekly, and monthly directories.
rules.impact: Write access for unprivileged users can enable privilege escalation through malicious scheduled jobs. Read access may reveal how elevated privileges are obtained or how audit controls can be bypassed.

rules.title: Crontab access is configured
rules.explanation: crontab installs, removes, and lists the job tables used by the cron daemon for per-user scheduled tasks.
rules.impact: Many environments restrict scheduled job creation to administrators. Controlling access with cron.allow enforces that policy and reduces the risk of unauthorized job scheduling.

rules.title: At access is configured
rules.explanation: The at utility schedules one-time jobs for later execution and supports flexible time specifications beyond basic POSIX.2 requirements.
rules.impact: Many environments restrict at job scheduling to administrators. Controlling access with at.allow enforces that policy and reduces the risk of unauthorized deferred command execution.

rules.title: Wireless interfaces are not available
rules.explanation: Wireless networking provides network connectivity when wired links are unavailable or impractical.
rules.impact: Unused wireless interfaces expand the local attack surface. Disabling wireless devices when wireless communication is not required reduces opportunities for unauthorized network access.

rules.title: Bluetooth services are not in use
rules.explanation: Bluetooth is a short-range wireless technology used to exchange data between nearby devices.
rules.impact: Unused Bluetooth services can expose systems to unauthorized proximity-based access and malware propagation between paired or discoverable devices, increasing the attack surface.
rules.scope: Settings in package bluez, systemd units

rules.title: The ATM kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) is a protocol that operates across network, data-link, and physical layers using virtual channels and virtual paths.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling the ATM kernel module when ATM is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The CAN kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: CAN (Controller Area Network) is a serial communication protocol originally developed for automotive and industrial control environments.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling the CAN kernel module when CAN is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The DCCP kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol) is a transport-layer protocol designed for streaming media and telephony workloads.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling the DCCP kernel module when DCCP is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The TIPC kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: TIPC (Transparent Inter-Process Communication) provides communication services intended for use between cluster nodes.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling the TIPC kernel module when TIPC is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The RDS kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: RDS (Reliable Datagram Sockets) is a transport-layer protocol designed for low-latency, high-throughput communication between cluster nodes.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling the RDS kernel module when RDS is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: The SCTP kernel module is not available
rules.explanation: SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) is a transport-layer protocol that supports message-oriented communication with multiple streams in a single association.
rules.impact: Unnecessary protocol support increases the local attack surface. Disabling the SCTP kernel module when SCTP is not required reduces that exposure.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.ip_forward is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv4.ip_forward parameter controls whether the system may forward IPv4 packets between network interfaces.
rules.impact: IP forwarding is appropriate for routers but unnecessary on most hosts. Leaving forwarding enabled can expose or advertise network topology and allow the host to route traffic unexpectedly. Setting net.ipv4.ip_forward to 0 prevents a multi-interface system from forwarding IPv4 packets.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.forwarding controls IPv4 packet forwarding across all network interfaces.
rules.impact: Forwarding capabilities are typically reserved for routers that exchange topology information with other routers. Enabling forwarding when it is not required can cause the system to participate in routing unexpectedly and expose network information.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.forwarding controls IPv4 packet forwarding for newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Forwarding capabilities are typically reserved for routers. Enabling default forwarding when it is not required can cause newly added interfaces to route traffic unexpectedly and expose network information.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects controls whether IPv4 ICMP Redirect messages are sent on all network interfaces.
rules.impact: A compromised host can send forged ICMP redirects to manipulate routing decisions and divert users to attacker-controlled systems instead of legitimate destinations.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects controls whether IPv4 ICMP Redirect messages are sent on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: A compromised host can send forged ICMP redirects to manipulate routing decisions and divert users to attacker-controlled systems instead of legitimate destinations.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses controls whether the kernel logs ICMP responses that do not conform to RFC 1122, such as bogus replies to broadcast frames.
rules.impact: Routers or attackers can generate non-compliant ICMP replies that flood logs with useless messages. Ignoring bogus error responses helps protect log storage and reduces noise that can obscure real incidents.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts controls whether the host ignores ICMP echo and timestamp requests sent to broadcast or multicast addresses.
rules.impact: Responding to broadcast or multicast echo requests can cause the host to participate in Smurf-style amplification attacks and increase unnecessary network load.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: ICMP Redirect messages convey alternate-path routing information to hosts. net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects controls whether IPv4 ICMP Redirect packets are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP redirects allows external hosts to influence the system routing table. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0 prevents unsolicited updates that could redirect traffic through attacker-controlled paths.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects controls whether newly added IPv4 network interfaces accept ICMP redirect packets that attempt to alter routing decisions.
rules.impact: Accepting ICMP redirects can allow a remote attacker to manipulate the host routing table. Disabling acceptance on default interfaces reduces this redirection risk for new interfaces.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are ICMP redirects that originate from gateways listed in the default gateway list. net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects controls whether these redirects are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Even known gateways may be compromised. Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects to 0 prevents routing-table updates from potentially untrusted gateways.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: Secure ICMP redirects are redirect messages that claim to come from gateways listed as default gateways. net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects controls acceptance of these messages on newly added interfaces.
rules.impact: Even known gateways can be compromised or spoofed. Disabling secure redirects on default interfaces prevents routing table updates from potentially untrusted gateway advertisements.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter enables reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on all network interfaces, verifying that inbound packets arrive on an expected interface for their source address.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter to 1 helps drop spoofed packets that would not be answerable via the receiving path. Note that asymmetric routing environments may require careful evaluation of this setting.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter enables reverse-path filtering for IPv4 traffic on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Setting net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter to 1 helps prevent acceptance of spoofed packets that would not be answerable via the receiving path on new interfaces.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route controls whether IPv4 interfaces accept packets that specify Strict or Loose Source Routing options.
rules.impact: Source-routed packets can be used to bypass intended network paths and security controls. Disabling acceptance of source routing reduces this attack vector on all IPv4 interfaces.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route controls whether newly added IPv4 interfaces accept packets with Strict or Loose Source Routing options.
rules.impact: Source-routed packets can bypass intended routing and filtering. Disabling acceptance on default interfaces prevents newly added interfaces from honoring source routes.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians controls whether IPv4 packets with impossible or non-routable source addresses are logged in the kernel log for all interfaces.
rules.impact: Logging martian packets helps administrators detect spoofed or malformed traffic that may indicate reconnaissance or attack activity against the system.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians controls whether IPv4 packets with impossible or non-routable source addresses are logged in the kernel log for newly added interfaces.
rules.impact: Logging martian packets on new interfaces helps administrators detect spoofed or malformed traffic that may indicate reconnaissance or attack activity.

rules.title: Net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies is configured
rules.explanation: When tcp_syncookies is enabled, the kernel handles TCP SYN packets normally until the connection queue is full, after which SYN cookie handling protects new connection attempts.
rules.impact: SYN flood attacks exhaust connection queues by sending many SYN packets without completing the handshake. Enabling SYN cookies allows the system to continue accepting legitimate connections during denial-of-service conditions.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding parameter controls whether the system may forward IPv6 packets between network interfaces.
rules.impact: IPv6 forwarding is appropriate for routers but unnecessary on most hosts. Leaving it enabled can expose network topology and allow unexpected routing. Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding to 0 prevents a multi-interface system from forwarding IPv6 packets.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding is configured
rules.explanation: The net.ipv6.conf.default.forwarding parameter controls whether newly added or default network interfaces may forward IPv6 packets.
rules.impact: IPv6 forwarding is typically reserved for routers. Enabling it when not required can cause the system to advertise or route network information unexpectedly.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects controls whether IPv6 ICMP Redirect packets are accepted on all network interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting IPv6 redirects allows external hosts to influence system routing. Setting net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects to 0 prevents outsiders from updating the routing table through redirect messages.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects controls whether newly added IPv6 interfaces accept ICMP redirect packets that attempt to alter routing decisions.
rules.impact: Accepting IPv6 ICMP redirects can allow manipulation of the host routing table. Disabling acceptance on default interfaces reduces redirection risk for new IPv6 interfaces.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route controls whether IPv6 interfaces accept packets that specify source routing options.
rules.impact: Source-routed IPv6 packets can be used to bypass intended network paths. Disabling acceptance reduces this attack vector on all IPv6 interfaces.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route is configured
rules.explanation: net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route controls whether newly added IPv6 interfaces accept packets with source routing options.
rules.impact: Source-routed packets can bypass intended routing and filtering. Disabling acceptance on default interfaces prevents newly added IPv6 interfaces from honoring source routes.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send multicast Router Advertisement (RA) messages to announce availability and provide autoconfiguration information to neighboring nodes. net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra controls whether these messages are accepted on all interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting unsolicited router advertisements can cause a host to route traffic through attacker-controlled systems. Disabling RA acceptance reduces the risk of malicious network reconfiguration.

rules.title: Net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra is configured
rules.explanation: Routers periodically send multicast Router Advertisement (RA) messages to announce availability and provide autoconfiguration information. net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra controls whether these messages are accepted on newly added network interfaces.
rules.impact: Accepting unsolicited router advertisements can cause a host to route traffic through attacker-controlled systems. Disabling RA acceptance on new interfaces reduces the risk of malicious network reconfiguration.

rules.title: Firewalld is installed
rules.explanation: firewalld is a dynamic firewall management utility that configures packet filtering through the Linux kernel nftables subsystem. It provides zones, services, and a D-Bus interface for runtime rule changes without disrupting existing connections.
rules.impact: A properly managed host firewall reduces exposure to network-borne threats, including unauthorized remote access and malicious traffic from adjacent systems. Without firewalld, administrators lack a consistent, supported mechanism to enforce host-based network controls.

rules.title: Firewalld backend is configured
rules.explanation: The FirewallBackend option in firewalld selects the underlying packet-filtering implementation used to enforce firewall rules.
rules.impact: An incorrect or unsupported backend can prevent firewall rules from being applied as intended, leaving the host unprotected. Verifying the backend configuration ensures that firewalld can enforce critical network controls reliably.

rules.title: Firewalld.service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: firewalld.service is the systemd unit that runs the firewalld daemon, providing a dynamically configurable host firewall with a D-Bus interface.
rules.impact: If firewalld.service is not active, configured firewall rules are not enforced. If it is not enabled, the firewall will not start automatically after reboot, leaving the system exposed until the service is started manually.

rules.title: Firewalld active zone target is configured
rules.explanation: Firewalld zones define the trust level applied to network interfaces and connections. The zone target determines the default disposition for packets that do not match an explicit allow rule and may be set to ACCEPT, %%REJECT%%, or DROP.
rules.impact: A default ACCEPT policy allows any traffic not explicitly denied, which expands the attack surface. Configuring a restrictive zone target (REJECT or DROP) ensures that only explicitly permitted traffic is accepted, reducing unintended network exposure.

rules.title: Access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/ssh/sshd_config file and *.conf files under /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d contain configuration settings for the OpenSSH server (sshd).
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of sshd configuration can weaken authentication, encryption, or access controls. Restricting permissions on these files helps prevent unprivileged users from altering SSH security settings.

rules.title: Access to SSH host private key files is configured
rules.explanation: SSH host private key files are used by the SSH server to prove the host identity during the SSH handshake and form one half of the host key pair used in public-key authentication of the host.
rules.impact: Compromise of an SSH host private key allows an attacker to impersonate the host, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks and undermining trust in SSH connections. Strict permissions help protect these keys from unauthorized access.

rules.title: Access to SSH host public key files is configured
rules.explanation: SSH host public key files correspond to the host private keys and are presented to clients during the SSH handshake to verify the server identity.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of host public key files can disrupt SSH trust relationships or facilitate host impersonation. Protecting these files reduces the risk of SSH service compromise through key tampering.

rules.title: Sshd access is configured
rules.explanation: OpenSSH provides directives such as AllowUsers, AllowGroups, DenyUsers, and DenyGroups to restrict which users and groups may authenticate to the SSH service.
rules.impact: Without access restrictions, any valid local account may attempt remote SSH login. Limiting SSH access to authorized users and groups reduces the risk of unauthorized remote access and narrows the attack surface.

rules.title: Sshd Banner is configured
rules.explanation: The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents are displayed to the remote client before authentication is allowed.
rules.impact: A pre-login banner communicates site-specific connection and acceptable-use policy to connecting users. Displaying a legal warning before authentication can support accountability and assist in prosecuting unauthorized access.

rules.title: Sshd Ciphers are configured
rules.explanation: The Ciphers directive restricts which symmetric encryption algorithms SSH may negotiate for protecting session confidentiality.
rules.impact: Weak or outdated ciphers may fail to provide adequate confidentiality or integrity for SSH sessions. Restricting SSH to strong ciphers reduces the risk that session data can be intercepted or altered.

rules.title: Sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
rules.explanation: ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax control how the SSH server detects and terminates idle or unresponsive client sessions through keepalive messages.
rules.impact: Sessions left open indefinitely consume resources and may be hijacked if a user leaves a connection unattended. Appropriate timeout values reduce the risk of resource exhaustion and limit the window for unauthorized use of abandoned sessions.

rules.title: Sshd DisableForwarding is enabled
rules.explanation: The DisableForwarding parameter disables all SSH forwarding features, including X11 forwarding, ssh-agent forwarding, TCP forwarding, and StreamLocal forwarding.
rules.impact: Forwarding features can be abused to tunnel traffic through the SSH host, bypass network controls, or establish covert channels. Disabling forwarding reduces the attack surface unless a documented operational need exists.

rules.title: Sshd GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: The GSSAPIAuthentication parameter controls whether users may authenticate to SSH using GSSAPI-based mechanisms such as Kerberos.
rules.impact: Enabling GSSAPI authentication exposes additional authentication pathways from remote hosts. Disabling it when not required reduces the system attack surface and limits dependency on external authentication infrastructure.

rules.title: Sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
rules.explanation: HostbasedAuthentication permits authentication based on trusted hosts using mechanisms historically associated with .rhosts or /etc/hosts.equiv style trust.
rules.impact: Host-based authentication is weaker than user-centric methods and can be abused if host trust relationships are compromised. Disabling it provides defense in depth even when related PAM or rhosts support is already limited.

rules.title: Sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
rules.explanation: The IgnoreRhosts parameter causes sshd to ignore .rhosts and .shosts files during RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.
rules.impact: Ignoring .rhosts and .shosts files prevents weak host-trust based authentication paths from being used. This reduces the risk of unauthorized access through manipulated or legacy trust files.

rules.title: Sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
rules.explanation: KexAlgorithms defines the key exchange methods SSH may use to establish shared session keys between client and server before encrypted communication begins.
rules.impact: Weak key exchange algorithms—those with insufficient key strength or weak hash functions—can expose SSH sessions to man-in-the-middle and related cryptographic attacks. Restricting KexAlgorithms to strong methods protects the integrity of the handshake.

rules.title: Sshd LoginGraceTime is configured
rules.explanation: LoginGraceTime specifies how long the SSH server allows a connection to remain unauthenticated before disconnecting the client.
rules.impact: A long grace period increases the opportunity for brute-force authentication attempts and can allow many concurrent unauthenticated connections. A reasonably short LoginGraceTime reduces these risks and limits resource consumption by incomplete logins.

rules.title: Sshd LogLevel is configured
rules.explanation: LogLevel controls the verbosity of OpenSSH server logging, ranging from minimal messages to detailed diagnostic output.
rules.impact: Adequate SSH logging supports detection and investigation of unauthorized access attempts. Levels such as INFO or VERBOSE capture login activity—and at VERBOSE, key fingerprints used for authentication—improving auditability without excessive noise.

rules.title: Sshd MACs are configured
rules.explanation: The MACs directive restricts which message authentication code algorithms SSH may use to protect the integrity of encrypted session data.
rules.impact: Weak MAC algorithms, including MD5-based and 96-bit MACs, have been associated with SSH downgrade and related cryptographic attacks. Restricting MACs to strong algorithms reduces the risk of session tampering and cryptographic compromise.

rules.title: Sshd MaxAuthTries is configured
rules.explanation: MaxAuthTries specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted per SSH connection before the connection is terminated.
rules.impact: Unlimited or high authentication attempt limits facilitate password guessing and brute-force attacks against SSH. A low MaxAuthTries value reduces the effectiveness of such attacks per connection.

rules.title: Sshd MaxStartups is configured
rules.explanation: MaxStartups limits the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections that the SSH daemon will accept, with optional rate-limiting behavior as connections approach the limit.
rules.impact: A flood of unauthenticated SSH connections can exhaust resources and degrade or deny legitimate login availability. Configuring MaxStartups mitigates denial-of-service risk against sshd.

rules.title: Sshd MaxSessions is configured
rules.explanation: MaxSessions specifies the maximum number of open sessions permitted for a single SSH connection.
rules.impact: Excessive concurrent sessions on a single connection can consume resources and contribute to denial of service. Limiting MaxSessions helps preserve sshd availability and prevent daemon overload.

rules.title: Sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitEmptyPasswords controls whether the SSH server allows login to accounts that have an empty password string.
rules.impact: Accounts with empty passwords can be accessed without credentials, enabling trivial unauthorized remote access. Disabling PermitEmptyPasswords reduces the likelihood of unauthenticated shell access via SSH.

rules.title: Sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitRootLogin controls whether the root account may authenticate directly over SSH.
rules.impact: Direct root SSH logins obscure individual accountability and concentrate risk on a single privileged credential. Requiring administrators to log in with individual accounts and then escalate privileges improves non-repudiation and audit trails during security incidents.

rules.title: Sshd PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
rules.explanation: PermitUserEnvironment allows users to set environment variables for their SSH sessions via environment files processed by the SSH daemon.
rules.impact: User-controlled environment variables passed through sshd can be used to alter program behavior and potentially bypass security controls. Disabling this option reduces that risk.

rules.title: Sshd UsePAM is enabled
rules.explanation: The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) interface for SSH authentication, account, and session management.
rules.impact: When UsePAM is enabled, SSH leverages system PAM policy for account and session handling, ensuring consistent enforcement of local authentication controls such as lockouts and password policies.

rules.title: Sudo is installed
rules.explanation: sudo allows an authorized user to execute a command as the superuser or another user according to a configured security policy.
rules.impact: Without sudo, privilege escalation often depends on shared root credentials or unrestricted su use, which weakens accountability. Installing sudo enables controlled, auditable privilege elevation based on defined policy.

rules.title: Sudo commands use pty
rules.explanation: sudo can be configured to require that commands run only from a pseudo-terminal (pty), preventing execution in environments without a controlling terminal.
rules.impact: Without a pty requirement, attackers may abuse sudo to launch malicious programs that spawn background processes persisting after the main command exits. Requiring a pty reduces this class of privilege-abuse techniques.

rules.title: Sudo logfile is configured
rules.explanation: The Defaults logfile setting specifies a dedicated file path where sudo records command execution activity.
rules.impact: A dedicated sudo log file simplifies review of privileged command use and supports creation of auditd rules focused on sudo activity. This improves detection and investigation of unauthorized privilege escalation.

rules.title: Users must provide a password for privilege escalation
rules.explanation: The system must require users to authenticate with a password when elevating privileges through mechanisms such as sudo, rather than allowing passwordless escalation.
rules.impact: Without reauthentication at privilege escalation, an unattended or compromised user session may be used to perform unauthorized administrative actions. Requiring a password reduces that risk and reinforces accountability.

rules.title: Sudo re-authentication is not disabled globally
rules.explanation: sudo can be configured with timestamp and authentication options that control whether users must re-authenticate for privilege escalation. Globally disabling re-authentication removes that verification for subsequent sudo use within the timestamp window policy.
rules.impact: If re-authentication is disabled globally, a compromised user session may retain elevated access without presenting credentials again, increasing the impact of session hijacking.

rules.title: Sudo timestamp_timeout is configured
rules.explanation: sudo caches successful authentication credentials for a period defined by timestamp_timeout (five minutes by default) so that subsequent sudo invocations may not immediately require reauthentication.
rules.impact: A long or unlimited credential cache widens the window in which another person could use an authenticated sudo session. Configuring an appropriate timeout reduces the opportunity for unauthorized privileged access.

rules.title: Access to the su command is restricted
rules.explanation: The su command allows a user to run a shell or command as another user. By default, any local user may attempt to invoke su.
rules.impact: Unrestricted su use enables broader attempts to obtain other accounts' privileges, including root. Restricting su—typically in favor of sudo—gives administrators stronger control over privilege elevation.

rules.title: Active authselect profile includes PAM modules
rules.explanation: authselect manages system authentication profiles. A custom profile can be created by copying and customizing a default profile so that required PAM modules and options can be configured.
rules.impact: Many PAM security settings require a custom authselect profile. Changes made directly to default profiles may be overwritten during updates, potentially reverting hardening and weakening authentication controls.

rules.title: Pam_faillock module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_faillock.so module tracks failed authentication attempts per user over a defined interval and locks the account when consecutive failures exceed the configured threshold.
rules.impact: Account lockout after repeated failed logons slows password-guessing and brute-force attacks. Enabling pam_faillock strengthens authentication defenses against credential stuffing and online password attacks.

rules.title: Pam_pwquality module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality.so module performs password quality checking when users set or change passwords, enforcing complexity and related strength requirements.
rules.impact: Weak passwords are easier to guess or crack. Enforcing password quality increases the time and resources required for successful password attacks and improves overall account security.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_pwhistory.so module stores recent user passwords and prevents reuse of those passwords within the configured history depth.
rules.impact: Password reuse allows attackers who obtain an old or compromised password to regain access after a forced change. Enforcing password history reduces that risk.

rules.title: Pam_unix module is enabled
rules.explanation: The pam_unix.so module is the standard Unix PAM module for authenticating users against local account credentials and updating traditional Unix password hashes.
rules.impact: Local authentication through pam_unix ensures that users must present valid credentials to access the system. Without it, core password-based authentication controls may not function as intended.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts is configured
rules.explanation: The deny option used with account lockout (for example via pam_faillock) denies access when consecutive failed authentications for a user within the configured interval exceed the specified threshold.
