rules.impact: Limiting consecutive failed logon attempts reduces the effectiveness of password-guessing attacks. Configured lockout thresholds help protect accounts from online brute-force authentication.

rules.title: Password unlock time is configured
rules.explanation: Unlock time defines how long an account remains locked after exceeding the failed authentication threshold before access may be restored automatically.
rules.impact: Without a defined unlock interval, lockout behavior may be ineffective or inconsistent. An appropriate unlock time sustains protection against password-guessing while allowing legitimate recovery after temporary lockouts.

rules.title: Lockout after failed password attempts includes the root account
rules.explanation: pam_faillock can lock accounts after consecutive failed authentication attempts. Including the root account ensures the same lockout controls apply to direct root logon attempts.
rules.impact: Excluding root from lockout allows unlimited password guessing against the most privileged account. Applying lockout to root reduces brute-force risk against administrative access.

rules.title: Password difok (changed characters) is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality difok setting requires a minimum number of characters in a new password to differ from the previous password.
rules.impact: Without a sufficient change requirement, users may make trivial password modifications that remain easy to guess. Enforcing difok strengthens password rotation effectiveness.

rules.title: Password length is configured
rules.explanation: The minlen parameter sets the minimum acceptable length for a new password during password quality checks.
rules.impact: Short passwords are significantly easier to compromise through guessing and brute-force attacks. Enforcing a minimum length strengthens resistance to credential attacks.

rules.title: Password complexity is configured
rules.explanation: Password complexity requirements can be enforced using parameters such as minclass, dcredit, ucredit, ocredit, and lcredit to require diverse character classes in new passwords.
rules.impact: Passwords lacking character diversity are more susceptible to brute-force and dictionary attacks. Enforcing complexity requirements increases password strength and reduces the likelihood of successful credential compromise.

rules.title: Password maxrepeat is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality maxrepeat setting limits how many identical consecutive characters are allowed in a new password.
rules.impact: Passwords with long runs of the same character are weaker and easier to guess. Limiting consecutive repeats improves password strength against common weak patterns.

rules.title: Password maxsequence is configured
rules.explanation: The pam_pwquality maxsequence setting limits sequential character runs (such as abcd or 1234) allowed in a new password.
rules.impact: Sequential character patterns are common and easily guessed. Limiting sequences reduces predictable password choices.

rules.title: Password dictionary checking is enabled
rules.explanation: The dictcheck parameter controls whether candidate passwords are checked against the cracklib dictionary of common or weak words.
rules.impact: Dictionary-based passwords are frequently targeted in guessing and brute-force attacks. Enabling dictionary checking reduces the chance that users select easily cracked passwords.

rules.title: Password quality is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: When enforce_for_root is enabled, pam_pwquality returns an error on failed quality checks even when the password being changed belongs to the root account.
rules.impact: Weak root passwords present a high-impact risk because root controls the entire system. Enforcing password quality for root increases the effort required to crack the privileged credential.

rules.title: Password history remembering is configured
rules.explanation: Previous passwords are stored in /etc/security/opasswd and checked to prevent reuse. The remember argument sets how many prior passwords are retained for history enforcement.
rules.impact: Requiring users not to reuse recent passwords reduces the likelihood that an attacker can reuse a guessed or previously compromised password after a password change.

rules.title: Password history is enforced for the root user
rules.explanation: When pwhistory enforce_for_root is enabled, the pam_pwhistory module applies password history checks to the root account as well as ordinary users.
rules.impact: Root password reuse carries elevated risk because the account has unrestricted privileges. Enforcing history for root reduces the chance that a previously compromised root password remains valid after rotation.

rules.title: Pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option forces pam_pwhistory, when changing a password, to use the new password already provided by a previously stacked password module rather than prompting again.
rules.impact: use_authtok ensures password modules in the PAM stack operate on the same confirmed new password, preserving consistent enforcement of history and quality checks before the password is accepted.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include nullok
rules.explanation: The nullok argument overrides the default pam_unix.so behavior that denies access when a user's password is empty, allowing authentication with a blank password.
rules.impact: Empty passwords provide no authentication strength and enable unauthorized access. Removing nullok helps ensure that accounts cannot authenticate without a password.

rules.title: Pam_unix does not include remember
rules.explanation: The remember=n argument to pam_unix stores the last n passwords in /etc/security/opasswd for history checking. Password history should be handled by pam_pwhistory rather than pam_unix.
rules.impact: Using remember with pam_unix can interfere with strong password hashing and duplicates history functionality better provided by pam_pwhistory. Removing remember from pam_unix supports proper hashing and cleaner PAM configuration.

rules.title: Pam_unix uses a strong password hashing algorithm
rules.explanation: pam_unix stores and verifies local password hashes. The hashing algorithm option selects the cryptographic method used when passwords are created or updated.
rules.impact: Weak password hashes are easier to crack offline if /etc/shadow is disclosed. A strong hashing algorithm increases the cost of credential recovery for attackers.

rules.title: Pam_unix includes use_authtok
rules.explanation: The use_authtok option forces pam_unix, when changing a password, to use the new password provided by a previously stacked password module rather than prompting independently.
rules.impact: use_authtok allows stacked PAM modules to validate and confirm the same new password before it is committed, ensuring quality and history checks are applied consistently.

rules.title: Password maximum lifetime is configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs defines the maximum number of days a password may be used before it must be changed.
rules.impact: Limiting password lifetime reduces the window during which a compromised or guessed credential remains valid. Periodic expiration also limits prolonged use of weak or exposed passwords.

rules.title: Password minimum days between changes is configured
rules.explanation: PASS_MIN_DAYS in /etc/login.defs sets the minimum number of days that must elapse before a user is allowed to change their password again.
rules.impact: Without a minimum change interval, users can rapidly cycle through passwords to defeat history controls and return to a previous password. PASS_MIN_DAYS helps preserve the effectiveness of password reuse restrictions.

rules.title: Password expiration warning days are configured
rules.explanation: The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs specifies how many days before password expiration users are warned that their password will expire.
rules.impact: Advance notice of password expiration gives users time to choose a strong replacement password and reduces rushed or weak password changes that can undermine account security.

rules.title: A strong password hashing algorithm is configured
rules.explanation: ENCRYPT_METHOD in /etc/login.defs defines the default algorithm used to hash user passwords stored by the system.
rules.impact: Weaker hashing algorithms make offline password cracking more feasible if password hashes are obtained. SHA-512 and yescrypt provide stronger resistance to password cracking than legacy Linux hashing methods.

rules.title: Inactive password lock is configured
rules.explanation: INACTIVE defines the number of days after a password has expired during which the user may still log in and change the password before the account is locked for inactivity.
rules.impact: Inactive accounts are less likely to be monitored for failed logons or other anomalies and may retain valid credentials unused for long periods. Locking inactive accounts reduces the risk that dormant credentials are abused.

rules.title: Last password change date is in the past for all users
rules.explanation: Each user account records the date of the last password change. That date must be in the past for password aging policies to apply correctly.
rules.impact: A last password change date set in the future can cause password expiration controls to be bypassed or delayed. Ensuring dates are in the past preserves the effectiveness of configured password lifetime policies.

rules.title: Root is the only UID 0 account
rules.explanation: Any account with UID 0 has unrestricted superuser privileges on the system, equivalent to the root account.
rules.impact: Multiple UID 0 accounts expand the set of credentials that grant full system control and complicate accountability. Restricting UID 0 to root reduces privilege sprawl and the risk of unauthorized superuser access.

rules.title: Root is the only account with GID 0 as primary group
rules.explanation: GID 0 identifies the privileged root group. The root account's primary group membership should be GID 0, and ordinary accounts should not use GID 0 as their primary group.
rules.impact: Assigning GID 0 as a primary group to non-root accounts can grant unintended access to root-group-owned files. Keeping GID 0 associated with root helps prevent accidental or unauthorized privileged group access.

rules.title: Root is the only group with GID 0
rules.explanation: GID 0 identifies the primary administrative group, conventionally named root. Only that group should own GID 0.
rules.impact: Additional groups with GID 0 inherit root-equivalent group privileges, undermining separation of privilege and accountability.

rules.title: Access to the root account is controlled
rules.explanation: The root account may be accessed through several local and remote methods. If root has no password (or equivalent authentication control), any local user may be able to obtain full system control.
rules.impact: Uncontrolled root access equates to complete system compromise. Ensuring root authentication is properly set protects the highest-privilege account from unauthorized use.

rules.title: Integrity of the root PATH
rules.explanation: The PATH environment variable determines which directories are searched when root executes commands. An insecure PATH can cause unintended programs to be run with superuser privileges.
rules.impact: Including the current directory (.) or other writable directories in root's PATH enables Trojan horse attacks in which an administrator inadvertently executes a malicious program as root. A clean PATH reduces the risk of privilege escalation through path manipulation.
rules.scope: Settings in the PATH variable for root

rules.title: Root user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The umask (user file-creation mode mask) determines the default permission bits removed when the root user creates new files and directories.
rules.impact: An overly permissive root umask can create world- or group-writable sensitive files by default. A secure umask reduces accidental exposure of privileged files and directories.

rules.title: System accounts do not have a valid login shell
rules.explanation: System accounts shipped with the distribution are intended to run services and manage applications, not to provide interactive logins. Their login shells should be set to a non-interactive shell such as nologin.
rules.impact: Interactive shells on system accounts expand the attack surface if those credentials are compromised. Ensuring system accounts cannot obtain an interactive shell limits lateral movement and unauthorized interactive use.

rules.title: Accounts without a valid login shell are locked
rules.explanation: Distribution-provided and administrator-created accounts that are not intended for interactive use should have non-login shells and be locked so they cannot authenticate interactively.
rules.impact: Accounts not meant for interactive use may still be abused for authentication if left unlocked. Locking such accounts reduces the risk of unauthorized interactive or service-mediated access.

rules.title: Nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
rules.explanation: /etc/shells lists full paths of shells considered valid for user login. Utilities such as chsh consult this file when changing a user's shell.
rules.impact: If nologin is listed in /etc/shells, accounts configured with nologin may be treated as having a valid interactive shell. Removing nologin from /etc/shells helps ensure non-login accounts remain non-interactive.

rules.title: Default user shell timeout is configured
rules.explanation: TMOUT is a shell environment setting that defines an idle timeout in seconds after which an interactive shell session is terminated.
rules.impact: Unattended shell sessions can be hijacked by anyone with physical or remote access to the terminal. A default timeout reduces the window for unauthorized use and frees resources held by idle sessions.

rules.title: Default user umask is configured
rules.explanation: The umask (user file-creation mode mask) determines the default permission bits removed when users create new files and directories.
rules.impact: A permissive default umask can cause newly created files to be readable or writable by unintended users. A secure default umask reduces accidental information disclosure and unauthorized modification.

rules.title: AIDE is installed
rules.explanation: AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) creates a baseline of files and directories—including attributes such as modification times, permissions, and cryptographic hashes—and later compares the live filesystem against that baseline to detect changes.
rules.impact: Filesystem integrity monitoring helps detect unauthorized or accidental changes to critical files and binaries. Early detection limits the impact of compromise, tampering, or misconfiguration.

rules.title: Regular filesystem integrity checking
rules.explanation: AIDE (or an equivalent integrity tool) can periodically compare the filesystem against a known baseline of file attributes and cryptographic checksums.
rules.impact: Regular integrity checks help detect unauthorized changes to critical system files that may indicate compromise or unintended modification.

rules.title: Cryptographic mechanisms protect audit tool integrity
rules.explanation: Cryptographic integrity checking can protect audit tools and related binaries so that unauthorized modification is detectable. This is typically implemented with an integrity monitoring solution such as AIDE.
rules.impact: If audit tools are altered without detection, an attacker can conceal activity or falsify audit review results. Cryptographic integrity protection strengthens trust in audit tooling.

rules.title: Journald service is active
rules.explanation: The systemd-journald service collects and stores system and service log events in the systemd journal. Enabling and activating the service ensures logging begins at boot and continues during normal operation.
rules.impact: If systemd-journald is not active, the system may fail to capture logging events needed for troubleshooting, incident response, and security monitoring.

rules.title: Only one logging system is in use
rules.explanation: A host should rely on a single primary logging mechanism—either rsyslog or journald—as the authoritative log collector. Using one centralized approach avoids overlapping collectors writing the same events through different paths.
rules.impact: Running multiple logging systems concurrently can create redundancy, inconsistent configuration, wasted resources, and gaps or duplication that complicate monitoring and forensic analysis.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote is installed
rules.explanation: The systemd-journal-remote package provides components for sending journal events to a remote log host or receiving journal messages from remote systems. It supports centralized journal-based log management.
rules.impact: Remote log storage protects log integrity if a local host is compromised, helping ensure historical evidence remains available for investigation.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-upload is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The systemd-journal-upload service forwards journal events collected on the local system to a remote journal host. Enabling and activating the service establishes continuous remote upload of journal data.
rules.impact: Storing logs on a remote host reduces the risk that an attacker with local access can delete or alter evidence of malicious activity.

rules.title: Systemd-journal-remote service is not in use
rules.explanation: The systemd-journal-remote service receives journal messages from remote hosts, functioning as a log server. Client systems that only send logs should not run this receiving service.
rules.impact: Enabling journal reception on a client expands its role beyond intended boundaries and increases attack surface by accepting inbound log traffic that should be handled only by designated log servers.

rules.title: Journald ForwardToSyslog is disabled
rules.explanation: The ForwardToSyslog setting controls whether journald forwards collected messages to a traditional syslog daemon. When journald is the chosen logging method, journal data should remain within journald rather than being forwarded elsewhere.
rules.impact: Forwarding journal data to another logging mechanism can duplicate processing, create inconsistent retention, and undermine a single coherent logging architecture.

rules.title: Journald Compress is configured
rules.explanation: Journald can compress journal files to reduce the disk space consumed by stored logs. Compression helps keep large volumes of log data within available storage limits.
rules.impact: Uncompressed journal growth can exhaust filesystem space, causing resource unavailability and disrupting services that depend on free disk capacity.

rules.title: Journald storage is configured
rules.explanation: Journald can store log data in volatile memory or persistently on local disk. Persistent storage retains journal history across reboots according to configured retention settings.
rules.impact: Persistent on-disk journals enable forensic reconstruction of events after crashes or reboots, which volatile-only storage cannot provide.

rules.title: Rsyslog is installed
rules.explanation: The rsyslog package provides a flexible syslog implementation for collecting, filtering, and writing system logs. It is used where traditional or centralized syslog-based logging is required instead of, or in addition to, journald.
rules.impact: Installing rsyslog enables a maintained, feature-rich logging stack needed for consistent log capture, remote forwarding, and security monitoring in environments that rely on rsyslog.

rules.title: Rsyslog service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: After the rsyslog package is installed, the rsyslog service must be enabled and running so that it starts at boot and continuously processes log messages.
rules.impact: If rsyslog is not enabled to start at boot, the system may fail to capture logging events required for security monitoring and operational diagnostics.

rules.title: Journald is configured to send logs to rsyslog
rules.explanation: systemd-journald can forward collected messages to rsyslog so that journal events are processed through the rsyslog pipeline. This configuration is used when rsyslog is the preferred system log collector.
rules.impact: Without forwarding, logs captured only in the journal may not reach rsyslog for further processing, archival, or remote shipping, creating incomplete visibility when rsyslog is the designated logging path.

rules.title: Rsyslog log file creation mode is configured
rules.explanation: When rsyslog creates new log files, the $FileCreateMode parameter sets the default permission mode applied to those files. This controls the initial access rights on newly created log destinations.
rules.impact: Incorrect creation modes can leave sensitive log data readable or writable by unauthorized users, weakening confidentiality and integrity of security-relevant records.

rules.title: Rsyslog is not configured to receive remote client logs
rules.explanation: rsyslog can be configured to accept log messages from remote clients, acting as a log server. Hosts that are not designated log collectors should not enable remote receive modules or listeners.
rules.impact: Accepting remote logs on a non-collector host expands the attack surface and can allow log injection or resource exhaustion from untrusted network sources.

rules.title: Access to all log files is configured
rules.explanation: Log files contain output from local system services and, on a centralized log host, may also contain logs from remote systems. Access controls on these files restrict which users and groups can read or modify them.
rules.impact: Excessive permissions on log files can expose sensitive data or allow tampering that obscures evidence of compromise; overly restrictive access can also impede legitimate administrative review.

rules.title: Auditd packages are installed
rules.explanation: auditd is the userspace component of the Linux audit subsystem and writes audit records to disk. Installing the audit packages provides the daemon and related tools needed for system event auditing.
rules.impact: Without auditd, administrators lack durable records of security-relevant system events needed to detect and investigate unauthorized access or policy violations.

rules.title: Processes that start before auditd are audited
rules.explanation: Early boot processes can run before auditd is fully started. Kernel audit parameters can ensure those early processes are still covered by the audit subsystem.
rules.impact: Without early auditing, malicious or unexpected activity during boot may leave no audit trail, creating a monitoring gap before auditd becomes active.

rules.title: Audit_backlog_limit is configured
rules.explanation: The audit_backlog_limit kernel parameter sets how many pending audit records can be held in the audit queue. An adequate limit is especially important early in boot when audit=1 may be enabled before auditd is fully ready.
rules.impact: If the backlog is too small during boot, audit records can be dropped, allowing potentially malicious activity to go unrecorded.

rules.title: Audit service is enabled and active
rules.explanation: The auditd daemon records security-relevant system events according to configured audit rules. Enabling and activating the service ensures auditing starts at boot and continues during operation.
rules.impact: If auditd is not running, the system will not generate the audit trail needed to detect unauthorized access and support accountability.

rules.title: Audit log storage size is configured
rules.explanation: auditd allows configuration of the maximum size of audit log files. Setting an appropriate max_log_file value balances retention needs against available disk capacity.
rules.impact: Without a defined maximum size, audit logs may grow until they impact system stability, or rotation behavior may be undefined, increasing the risk of lost or incomplete audit data.

rules.title: Audit logs are not deleted automatically
rules.explanation: The max_log_file_action parameter defines how auditd handles a log file that has reached its configured maximum size. High-security configurations retain logs rather than automatically deleting them.
rules.impact: Automatic deletion of audit logs can erase evidence needed for investigations; preserving audit history strengthens accountability and non-repudiation.

rules.title: System shuts down when audit logs are full
rules.explanation: auditd can be configured to halt the system or enter single-user mode when the partition holding audit logs has no free space or an error is detected. This fails closed rather than continuing without auditing.
rules.impact: In high-security environments, continuing to operate without space for audit records risks undetected unauthorized activity; availability is intentionally subordinated to preserving audit integrity.

rules.title: System warns when audit log space is low
rules.explanation: auditd can warn administrators, enter single-user mode, or halt when free space on the audit log partition falls below configured thresholds. Early warning provides time to free space or expand storage before auditing fails.
rules.impact: Without space warnings, audit logging can stop unexpectedly, creating gaps that undermine detection of unauthorized access and weaken non-repudiation.

rules.title: Changes to /etc/sudoers are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor modifications to /etc/sudoers and files under /etc/sudoers.d, which define sudo privilege scope for administrators and other users.
rules.impact: Unauthorized changes to sudoers configuration can expand or alter privileged access; auditing these changes supports detection of privilege escalation and policy tampering.

rules.title: Actions as another user are always logged
rules.explanation: sudo allows a user to run commands with elevated privileges or as another user. Logging these sessions records who used temporary privilege elevation and what operations were performed.
rules.impact: Without a complete audit trail of elevated or identity-switched commands, accountability for privileged actions is reduced and misuse is harder to detect.

rules.title: Events that modify the sudo log file are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor the sudo log file (commonly /var/log/sudo.log) for changes that indicate either legitimate sudo activity or tampering with the log itself.
rules.impact: Modifications to the sudo log may reflect administrative commands or intentional log alteration; collecting these events helps preserve accountability and detect cover-up attempts.

rules.title: Events that modify date and time information are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record system calls and related activity that change the system clock or time-related settings.
rules.impact: Unauthorized time changes can hide activity, disrupt authentication tokens, and undermine forensic timeline analysis. Auditing clock changes supports detection of such tampering.

rules.title: Events that modify the system hostname are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor sethostname and setdomainname system calls, which change the system's hostname and NIS/domain name.
rules.impact: Unexpected hostname or domain changes can indicate compromise or attempts to evade host-based monitoring and inventory controls.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor changes to /etc/issue and /etc/issue.net, which provide local and remote login banners presented before authentication.
rules.impact: Unauthorized banner changes can remove legal notices or present deceptive messages. Auditing these files helps detect tampering with login warning content.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/hosts and /etc/hostname are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor changes to /etc/hosts and /etc/hostname, which define local name resolution and the system hostname file.
rules.impact: Unauthorized changes can redirect traffic, spoof local names, or alter host identity, supporting man-in-the-middle or evasion techniques.

rules.title: Events that modify network configuration files are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor changes to /etc/sysconfig/network and NetworkManager connection profiles under /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/, which control network interface and routing behavior.
rules.impact: Unauthorized network configuration changes can redirect traffic, disable protections, or establish attacker persistence. Auditing these paths improves detection of such activity.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/NetworkManager are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record changes under /etc/NetworkManager, which contains NetworkManager configuration affecting how the system connects and routes traffic.
rules.impact: Unauthorized NetworkManager changes can alter connectivity and security posture. Auditing this directory helps detect malicious or accidental network policy changes.

rules.title: Use of privileged commands is collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor execution of programs with the setuid and/or setgid bits set, which run with elevated owner or group privileges. This helps identify when unprivileged users invoke privileged binaries.
rules.impact: Unexpected use of privileged commands by unprivileged users may indicate attempts to escalate privileges or otherwise gain unauthorized system access.

rules.title: Unsuccessful file access attempts are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules capture failed attempts to open, create, or truncate files. These events reflect access requests that were denied by permissions or other controls.
rules.impact: Patterns of failed file access can indicate reconnaissance or attempts to reach unauthorized data, supporting early detection of hostile activity.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/group are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record changes to /etc/group, which defines group names, GIDs, and membership used for access control.
rules.impact: Unauthorized group database changes can grant or remove privileges. Auditing /etc/group supports detection of privilege manipulation.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/passwd are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record changes to /etc/passwd, which defines local user accounts, UIDs, home directories, and login shells.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modifications to /etc/passwd can create backdoor accounts or alter identity mappings. Auditing these changes supports accountability and intrusion detection.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/shadow and /etc/gshadow are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record changes to /etc/shadow and /etc/gshadow, which store password hashes and related account and group security attributes.
rules.impact: Unexpected credential-store modifications may indicate account compromise or attempts to conceal attacker activity. Auditing these files strengthens detection of credential tampering.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/security/opasswd are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor /etc/security/opasswd, which stores previous password hashes when password history is enabled.
rules.impact: Tampering with password history files can defeat password reuse controls or expose historical credentials. Auditing changes helps detect such abuse.

rules.title: Events that modify /etc/nsswitch.conf are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor /etc/nsswitch.conf, which controls how the system resolves users, groups, hosts, and other databases through NSS.
rules.impact: Unauthorized NSS switch changes can redirect identity lookups to untrusted sources, undermining authentication and authorization integrity.

rules.title: Events that modify PAM configuration are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor /etc/pam.conf and files under /etc/pam.d/, which define authentication, account, password, and session stacks for system services.
rules.impact: Unauthorized PAM changes can weaken authentication requirements or introduce malicious modules. Auditing PAM configuration helps detect privilege and access-control tampering.

rules.title: DAC permission modification events are collected for chmod family calls
rules.explanation: Audit rules collect discretionary access control (DAC) permission changes made through chmod, fchmod, fchmodat, and related system calls.
rules.impact: Unexpected permission changes can expose sensitive files or enable privilege escalation. Auditing chmod-family calls helps detect unauthorized DAC modifications.

rules.title: DAC ownership modification events are collected for chown family calls
rules.explanation: Audit rules collect ownership changes made through chown, fchown, lchown, fchownat, and related system calls.
rules.impact: Unauthorized ownership changes can transfer control of critical files to an attacker. Auditing chown-family calls supports detection of DAC ownership abuse.

rules.title: DAC extended attribute modification events are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules collect changes to extended attributes through setxattr, lsetxattr, fsetxattr, removexattr, lremovexattr, and fremovexattr system calls.
rules.impact: Extended attribute changes can alter security labels or other access-related metadata. Auditing these calls helps detect unauthorized DAC and attribute tampering.

rules.title: Successful filesystem mounts are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules track successful use of the mount system call and related mount activity. This records when filesystems are attached to the directory tree.
rules.impact: Mounting filesystems, especially by unprivileged users, is uncommon and may indicate unauthorized access to removable media, backdoor placement, or bypass of intended access controls.

rules.title: Session initiation information is collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor session initiation records and related files that track when user sessions start. These events complement login auditing with session lifecycle detail.
rules.impact: Session initiation monitoring helps identify logons at unusual times or from unexpected contexts, which may indicate compromised credentials or attacker activity.

rules.title: Logon and logoff events are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules capture user logon and logoff events so that successful and failed authentication activity is recorded in the audit trail.
rules.impact: Logon and logoff records support detection of brute-force attempts, anomalous access patterns, and account misuse.

rules.title: File deletion events by users are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor system calls used to delete or rename files and related attributes. Collecting these events focuses on user-initiated removal or renaming of files.
rules.impact: Unauthorized deletion or renaming of protected files can destroy evidence or disrupt operations; auditing these calls helps detect improper file removal by unprivileged users.

rules.title: User file rename events are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor rename and related system calls that rename or move files, focusing on user-initiated filesystem object identity changes.
rules.impact: Unauthorized renaming can obscure evidence, disrupt applications, or move sensitive data. Auditing rename activity helps detect improper file manipulation.

rules.title: Events that modify mandatory access controls are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor changes related to the system's mandatory access control (MAC) policy, such as SELinux policy and context administration paths.
rules.impact: Unauthorized MAC policy changes can weaken confinement and allow privilege escalation. Auditing these events helps detect attempts to disable or bypass MAC protections.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful chcon command use is collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record successful and failed executions of the chcon command, which changes SELinux security contexts on files.
rules.impact: Misuse of chcon can weaken SELinux confinement for critical objects. Auditing both success and failure helps detect unauthorized context changes.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful setfacl command use is collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record successful and failed executions of the setfacl command, which modifies POSIX Access Control Lists on files and directories.
rules.impact: Unauthorized ACL changes can grant or remove access outside intended DAC policy. Auditing setfacl use helps detect privilege and access-control abuse.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful chacl command use is collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record successful and failed executions of the chacl command, which can modify Access Control Lists on filesystems that support it.
rules.impact: Unauthorized ACL manipulation can expand access to sensitive data. Auditing chacl activity supports detection of access-control tampering.

rules.title: Successful and unsuccessful usermod command use is collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules record successful and failed executions of the usermod command, which modifies user account attributes such as groups, shell, and home directory.
rules.impact: Unauthorized usermod activity can escalate privileges or create persistence through account changes. Auditing usermod helps detect account-management abuse.

rules.title: Kernel module load, unload, and changes via kmod are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules monitor use of /usr/bin/kmod and related module management utilities that load, unload, or otherwise manipulate kernel modules.
rules.impact: Unauthorized kernel module changes can introduce rootkits or weaken security controls. Auditing kmod usage provides evidence of potentially compromising kernel modifications.

rules.title: Kernel module init_module and finit_module events are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules collect init_module and finit_module system calls, which load kernel modules into the running kernel.
rules.impact: Unexpected module loads can alter kernel behavior and hide malicious activity. Auditing these system calls strengthens detection of unauthorized kernel code introduction.

rules.title: Kernel module delete_module events are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules collect the delete_module system call, which unloads kernel modules from the running kernel.
rules.impact: Unexpected module unloading can disable security features or remove forensic visibility. Auditing delete_module helps detect unauthorized kernel changes.

rules.title: Kernel module query_module events are collected
rules.explanation: Audit rules collect query_module-related activity used to inspect loaded kernel modules and module state.
rules.impact: Unusual module query patterns may indicate reconnaissance by malware or attackers preparing kernel-level persistence. Auditing these events supports early detection.

rules.title: Audit configuration loads independently of errors
rules.explanation: Audit rules can be configured so that the audit subsystem continues loading policy even when individual rule lines encounter errors, reducing the chance that a single mistake disables broader auditing.
rules.impact: If audit loading aborts on the first error, subsequent critical rules may never activate, creating monitoring gaps. Independent loading improves resilience of the audit configuration.

rules.title: Audit configuration is immutable
rules.explanation: The audit subsystem can be placed in immutable mode so that audit rules cannot be altered with auditctl until reboot. This locks the active rule set after it is loaded.
rules.impact: Immutable mode prevents an attacker from disabling or rewriting audit rules to conceal malicious activity and then restoring them before detection.

rules.title: Audit log directory mode is configured
rules.explanation: The audit log directory stores audit log files written by auditd. Its permission mode controls who can list, read, or write contents within that directory.
rules.impact: Weak directory permissions can allow unauthorized access to or tampering with audit records, settings, and reports required for reliable system activity auditing.

rules.title: Audit log file mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain detailed records of system and security-relevant activity. File mode settings restrict which users can read or modify those records.
rules.impact: Overly permissive modes can disclose sensitive system and configuration details to attackers, compromising the confidentiality of the audit trail.

rules.title: Audit log file owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain detailed records of system and security-relevant activity. Ownership should be restricted to the appropriate administrative identity that manages audit data.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership can grant unauthorized users control over audit records, enabling disclosure or alteration of evidence.

rules.title: Audit log file group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit log files contain detailed records of system and security-relevant activity. Group ownership should be limited to groups that legitimately require access for audit administration or review.
rules.impact: An incorrect group owner may expose audit records to unauthorized users, weakening confidentiality and integrity of the audit trail.

rules.title: Audit configuration file mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control auditd behavior and which events are audited. Restrictive file modes limit who can read or change those settings.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of audit configuration can disable auditing of critical events, allowing malicious activity to proceed without an audit trail.

rules.title: Audit configuration file owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control auditd behavior and which events are audited. Ownership should be restricted to the appropriate administrative identity.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership may allow unauthorized personnel to alter audit policy and prevent logging of critical security events.

rules.title: Audit configuration file group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit configuration files control auditd behavior and which events are audited. Group ownership should be limited to groups authorized to administer auditing.
rules.impact: An incorrect group owner can enable unauthorized changes that weaken or disable auditing of critical events.

rules.title: Audit tools mode is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools are the vendor-provided and open-source utilities used to review and manage audit records and system activity data. Their file modes restrict who can execute or modify these tools.
rules.impact: Unprotected audit tools can be altered or misused, undermining the integrity of audit administration and the reliability of log review.

rules.title: Audit tools owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools are the utilities used to review and manage audit records and system activity data. Ownership should be restricted to the appropriate administrative identity.
rules.impact: Incorrect ownership of audit tools can allow unauthorized modification or misuse, weakening protection of audit information.

rules.title: Audit tools group owner is configured
rules.explanation: Audit tools are the utilities used to review and manage audit records and system activity data. Group ownership should be limited to groups authorized for audit administration.
rules.impact: An incorrect group owner may permit unauthorized access to or alteration of tools required to manage and interpret audit data.

rules.title: Access to /etc/passwd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd file stores user account information consumed by many system utilities and must remain readable for normal system operation. Write access should be tightly restricted.
rules.impact: Unauthorized write access to /etc/passwd can alter accounts, change UIDs, or otherwise compromise authentication and access control.

rules.title: Access to /etc/passwd- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/passwd- file is a backup of user account information. It may contain the same sensitive account data as /etc/passwd and requires equivalent access protection.
rules.impact: Unauthorized access to /etc/passwd- can expose or allow modification of historical account data that attackers can misuse.

rules.title: Access to /etc/group is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group file lists valid groups defined on the system and is used by many programs. It must remain readable while write access is restricted to authorized administrators.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of /etc/group can alter group membership and privilege boundaries, while still requiring readability for legitimate system functions.

rules.title: Access to /etc/group- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/group- file is a backup of the system group list. It contains historical group definitions and should be protected like other account database files.
rules.impact: Unauthorized access to /etc/group- can expose or allow alteration of backup group data used to reconstruct or abuse group memberships.

rules.title: Access to /etc/shadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow file stores sensitive user account security data, including hashed passwords and related aging information. Access must be restricted to privileged accounts.
rules.impact: Read access to /etc/shadow enables offline password cracking against hashed credentials, accelerating account compromise.

rules.title: Access to /etc/shadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shadow- file is a backup of sensitive user account security information, including credential-related data. It requires the same strict access controls as /etc/shadow.
rules.impact: Unauthorized access to /etc/shadow- can expose historical password hashes and other account security data to attackers.

rules.title: Access to /etc/gshadow is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow file stores sensitive group security information, including hashed group passwords and related attributes. Access must be restricted to privileged accounts.
rules.impact: Read access to /etc/gshadow enables offline cracking of group password hashes and can facilitate unauthorized group privilege use.

rules.title: Access to /etc/gshadow- is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/gshadow- file is a backup of sensitive group security information. It should be protected with the same strict access controls as /etc/gshadow.
rules.impact: Unauthorized access to /etc/gshadow- can expose historical group credential data that attackers may use to escalate privileges.

rules.title: Access to /etc/shells is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/shells file lists full paths of valid login shells recognized by the system. It influences which interpreters may be used as login shells.
rules.impact: Unauthorized modification of /etc/shells can introduce untrusted shells or remove legitimate ones, affecting login security and account usability controls.

rules.title: Access to /etc/security/opasswd is configured
rules.explanation: The /etc/security/opasswd file and its backup /etc/security/opasswd.old store previous user passwords when pam_unix or pam_pwhistory password history is enabled. These files contain sensitive credential history.
rules.impact: Unauthorized access to password history files can expose prior credentials that users may still reuse, enabling account compromise.

rules.title: World-writable files and directories are protected
rules.explanation: World-writable files and directories can be modified by any local user. Locating and remediating unnecessary world-writable paths reduces shared writable attack surface on the filesystem.
rules.impact: World-writable locations allow any user to alter data or plant malicious content, and may indicate flawed software that can lead to broader integrity compromise.

rules.title: No unowned or ungrouped files or directories exist
rules.explanation: Every filesystem object should map to a valid user and group identity. Files or directories without an owner or group indicate orphaned ownership after account or group removal.
rules.impact: Unowned or ungrouped objects can become accessible in unexpected ways when UIDs or GIDs are reused, creating integrity and access-control risks.

rules.title: Accounts in /etc/passwd use shadow passwords
rules.explanation: Shadow password support stores password hashes in /etc/shadow rather than in the world-readable /etc/passwd file. Local accounts should use shadowed passwords so credentials are not exposed in /etc/passwd.
rules.impact: Password hashes in /etc/passwd are readable by all users and can be cracked offline; shadowing passwords protects credential confidentiality while keeping /etc/passwd readable for system utilities.

rules.title: /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
rules.explanation: An account with an empty password field in /etc/shadow can be accessed without providing a password. Every account should have a password hash or be locked so interactive login without credentials is not possible.
rules.impact: Empty password fields allow unauthorized login as that user, providing immediate unauthenticated access to the account and its privileges.

rules.title: All groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
rules.explanation: Each primary group GID referenced in /etc/passwd should correspond to a group defined in /etc/group. Orphaned GIDs indicate incomplete group database consistency.
rules.impact: Groups referenced in /etc/passwd but missing from /etc/group prevent proper group privilege management and can create unpredictable access-control behavior.

rules.title: No duplicate UIDs exist
rules.explanation: Each user account should have a unique UID so that ownership, permissions, and audit records map unambiguously to a single identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate UIDs break accountability and can grant unintended shared access to files and resources owned by that numeric identity.

rules.title: No duplicate GIDs exist
rules.explanation: Each group should have a unique GID so that group membership and group-based access controls map to a single group identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate GIDs undermine accountability and can cause unintended sharing of group privileges across distinct group names.

rules.title: No duplicate user names exist
rules.explanation: Each local user account should have a unique username so that authentication and authorization decisions apply to a single identity.
rules.impact: Duplicate usernames create ambiguity in access control and auditing, weakening accountability for user actions.

rules.title: No duplicate group names exist
rules.explanation: Each group should have a unique name so that membership and permission assignments resolve to a single group definition.
rules.impact: Duplicate group names create ambiguity in access control and weaken accountability for group-based privileges.

rules.title: Local interactive user home directories are configured
rules.explanation: Local interactive user accounts should have properly configured home directories with ownership and permissions appropriate for that user.
rules.impact: Missing or weakly protected home directories can expose user data or allow other users to plant malicious startup files that execute in the victim's context.

rules.title: Access to local interactive user dotfiles is configured
rules.explanation: Interactive users' dotfiles (such as shell startup files) configure the user environment and may contain sensitive settings or paths. These files should have permissions that prevent other users from reading or modifying them.
rules.impact: Excessive permissions on user dotfiles can allow attackers to steal or alter another user's configuration, potentially leading to data theft or privilege abuse within that user's context.
